newsitem.title: BELGIUM: West Europe car sales rise 5.2 percent in August.
newsitem.headline: West Europe car sales rise 5.2 percent in August.

text.p: New car sales in western Europe rose 5.2 percent in August year-on-year to 1,157,200 cars, following a 16.2 percent jump in July, the European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA) said on Thursday.
So far this year, new car registrations have increased by 6.2 percent to 9,083,400, ACEA said in a statement.
"There seems to be an upward trend, especially because of a couple of markets," said ACEA spokesman James Rosenstein.

France, which showed the strongest growth of all national markets in August with a rise of 28.6 percent, was affected by a state rebate scheme for new cars which was due to be phased out in September.
"So there is a lot of buying to take advantage of the incentive before it disappears," Rosenstein said.
The important German market, which increased by 5.2 percent, was driven by replacement demand and by the introduction of new models which were attracting buyers.

"Those are the two main markets that are driving the rest," Rosenstein said, adding that other markets -- such as Italy, where sales fell by 7.5 percent and Britain, where they rose by only 2.2 percent -- were not doing as well.

But he said the figure at the end of 1996 could be higher than ACEA originally expected. Growth for the year would probably be closer to four percent than three percent, which is still below the increase in the January-August period.
"We expect there to be somewhat of a slide towards the end of the year," Rosenstein said.
Jonathan Storey, director of European Automotive Research Ltd, said western Europe should now be in an "upward demand situation" following a drop of 16 percent in 1993.
Demand picked up in 1994 but was virtually flat last year. Storey expected registrations to grow by about four percent to 12.5 million units this year.
Rosenstein said the market was still depressed.
"But if you look at the longer trend it is picking up a little bit...the present trend is moderate growth," he said.
ACEA's August figures showed that most European car makers gained market shares while U.S. giants lost somewhat.
The Ford group, including luxury car maker Jaguar, recorded a drop of 4.2 percent to 155,266 cars.
But it was still one of the largest players in Europe with a market share of 13.4 percent, second only to Volkswagen.

Volkswagen, Europe's largest car maker, strengthened its position further, showing a 12.5 percent increase in new car registrations to 175,200 cars. Its market share firmed to 15.1 percent from 14.2 percent last year.
General Motors, including Opel and Saab, showed a decline of 1.9 percent. Its market share fell to 11.9 percent from 12.7.
In contrast, French firms PSA Peugeot Citroen and Renault saw new car registrations jump by 8.5 percent and 14.0 percent respectively, both boosting their market shares.
The Fiat and BMW groups also showed better figures.
However, Swedish car maker Volvo saw a decline of 3.7 percent to 15,220 cars compared with August last year.
The ACEA figures include the 15-nation European Union, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
